lead: Data security protects data through its lifecycle: classify it, control who can read it, encrypt or mask it where needed, keep it only as long as a policy allows, then delete or archive it safely. Data protection is the legal and policy duty to safeguard personal data and honour the data subject's rights, such as consent, purpose limitation and erasure. Data security is the set of technical and organisational controls that carry out that duty. Data retention is one rule inside that duty: it decides lifetime. Cloud storage makes copies cheap and fast, so deletion must reach backups, snapshots and replicas too. Use this when you design log retention, customer records, card data or tenant storage.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 cloud storage, replication and backups, and 6.3 encryption and key management.

blocks.text: Data classification labels data by sensitivity so controls can follow the label. Four common classes are public, internal, confidential and restricted. A public price list needs little control; a restricted customer record needs strict access and audit. Classification is the first step because you cannot protect every byte the same way without wasting money or slowing work.

items: Data loss prevention (DLP) inspects content and blocks or logs the movement of sensitive data, for example a card number leaving a web form.
Tokenization replaces a value with a token and keeps the real value in a separate vault. A payment service can store a token instead of a card number.
Redaction removes or masks fields before sharing data with test teams or reports.
Obfuscation replaces sensitive fields with realistic but false values while keeping the format, so tests still run.

blocks.text: Encryption is covered in 6.3, but the idea here is selective use. Encrypt restricted data at rest and in transit, tokenize values that must never sit in an application store, and redact before copying production data to a test environment. Access control decides who may read the data after these controls; that is 6.5 IAM.

sections.h3: Retention policy, legal hold and the log timeline

blocks.text: A retention policy states, for each data class, how long the data must exist, where it lives, who approves deletion and how it is deleted. Retention is a business and legal rule, not just the storage lifetime. A legal hold is a directive that suspends deletion for an investigation or dispute, even after the normal retention period ends.

blocks.where: R is the total stored volume at the end of the archive period, in GB (active copies plus compressed archive copies); Vd is the daily data volume in GB per day; Da is active days; Dr is archive days; C is the compression ratio. In the example, R = 1,175 GB at day 364, while storage at the end of the active period alone is Vd × Da = 900 GB.

blocks.text: Archiving moves older data to cheaper storage with metadata so it can be found. The worked example uses logs: 10 GB per day, 90 active days, then archive from day 90 to day 365 with 10:1 compression, then a purge window from day 365 to day 395. The figure shows the same timeline.

items: Name the data set and its owner.
Set the retention period and archive tier.
Define the deletion method and the approval step.
Record how a legal hold is raised, reviewed and released.

blocks.text: Deleting the live copy is not deletion if backups, snapshots or replicas still hold the data. A backup lifetime is the recovery window; it can differ from the retention period. A backup may outlive retention, so the deletion job must also expire backups and snapshots. Secure disposal of physical media and crypto-shredding, which destroys the key so ciphertext cannot be read, close the last copies.

items: Freeze new writes for the data set and open a deletion ticket.
Find every copy: live store, snapshots, backups, replicas, caches and search indexes.
Check legal holds; if a hold applies, stop.
Delete or crypto-shred each copy; verify by sampling.
Expire keys and media, then log the result for audit in 6.9.

blocks.text: Tenant data separation keeps one customer's data away from another in a shared cloud service. Use per-tenant encryption keys, separate partition keys or table prefixes, and IAM conditions that limit each request to one tenant. These controls must hold for backups and archives too, because a copy that ignores tenant labels leaks data even when the live store is correct.

figure.caption: Logs at 10 GB/day stay active for 90 days (900 GB), then archive from day 90 to day 365 at 10:1 compression (275 GB), then purge from day 365 to day 395. Notice the archive bar is the compressed 275 GB, not the raw 2,750 GB; at day 364 active plus archive is 1,175 GB, and the purge takes the day-365 log set to 0 GB.

spec.aria: A retention timeline for logs at 10 GB per day: active for 90 days at 900 GB, archived from day 90 to day 365 at 275 GB after 10:1 compression, then a purge window from day 365 to day 395 that removes the day-365 set to 0 GB; active plus archive at day 364 is 1,175 GB.

examples.question: A service writes 10 GB of logs per day. Logs stay active for 90 days. From day 90 to day 365 they are archived with 10:1 compression. A purge runs from day 365 to day 395. Compute the stored volume at day 364 (active plus archive) and the volume after purge.
steps: Daily volume Vd = 10 GB/day and active days Da = 90. Active storage = 10 × 90 = 900 GB.
Archive days Dr = 365 − 90 = 275 days. Raw archive = 10 × 275 = 2,750 GB.
Compression ratio C = 10. Compressed archive = 2,750 ÷ 10 = 275 GB.
Day 364 total = active + compressed archive = 900 + 275 = 1,175 GB.

The purge window from day 365 to day 395 removes the live and archive copies of the log set written up to day 365. Assume no new logs are counted. After purge = 0 GB. If logging continues, day 365 to day 395 adds 300 GB of new active logs; the purge removes only data older than the active window.
examples.answer: At day 364 the service stores 1,175 GB; after the purge window it stores 0 GB for the log set written up to day 365, assuming no new logs are counted.
examples.check:
daily = 10
active_days = 90
archive_days = 365 - 90
compression = 10
active = daily * active_days
archive_raw = daily * archive_days
archive_comp = archive_raw / compression
total = active + archive_comp
after_purge = 0
print(int(active))
print(int(archive_raw))
print(int(archive_comp))
print(int(total))
print(int(after_purge))

traps: Deleting the live copy is not deletion if backups, snapshots or replicas still hold the data.
Retention period and backup lifetime are different rules; a backup may outlive retention and must still expire.
Tokenization is not encryption: a token is a reference to a vault value, while encryption transforms the value itself.
A legal hold overrides scheduled deletion even after the retention period ends; deleting anyway destroys evidence.
Compression reduces stored GB, so divide the raw archive by the compression ratio; do not multiply.

quiz.a: Data classification groups data by sensitivity, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, so controls can follow the label.

quiz.q: Why can tokenization be safer than storing an encrypted card number in an application database?
quiz.a: Tokenization replaces the card number with a token mapped in a separate vault, so the sensitive value is not in the application store. Encryption still keeps the recoverable value there.

quiz.q: A service writes 5 GB of logs per day and keeps them active for 30 days with no archive. What is the active stored volume?
A retention policy says delete customer records after 1 year. A legal hold is active. What should the deletion job do and why?
quiz.a: It must stop deletion for held records. Legal hold suspends deletion for an investigation or dispute; deleting would destroy evidence and break policy.

quiz.q: Explain why deleting a live object may not satisfy a retention policy.
quiz.a: Backups, snapshots and replicas may still hold the object. Retention requires deletion of every copy, including backup expiry and archive copies.

quiz.q: What does DLP inspect and do?
quiz.a: Data loss prevention inspects content and blocks or logs the movement of sensitive data.

quiz.q: How does tenant data separation prevent a cross-tenant leak?
quiz.a: It uses separate keys, partitions, prefixes and IAM conditions so one tenant's request cannot read another tenant's objects, including backups.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry tools now express retention as machine-readable policy and apply it across object stores, databases and backups. Privacy engineering links retention to consent and data minimisation. Search for cloud data lifecycle management, crypto-shredding, DLP rules and legal hold automation. The hard part is proving deletion across every copy.
